articles.title: The Trees That Needed the Wind
articles.dek: In a sealed glass world in the Arizona desert, young trees grew fast and then fell over. Hebrews 12 explains why God still shakes the earth, and what he is keeping when he does.
articles.quote: When God shakes your life, he is sorting it, clearing away what was never strong enough to hold you so that what cannot be shaken may remain.
articles.body:
In September 1991, eight people stepped inside a sealed world in the Arizona desert and closed the door behind them for two years. Biosphere 2 was a three-acre structure of glass and steel built to test whether a complete living system could sustain itself, and inside it were a small rainforest, a saltwater ocean with its own coral reef, farm plots, and groves of young trees. The trees seemed to love it at first. Sheltered from the harsh weather outside, they grew faster than their cousins in the open air, until, well before they reached maturity, many of them began to bend, sag, and in some cases topple under their own weight.

The researchers eventually traced the problem to something no one had thought to include. The air inside the dome was almost perfectly still. Out in the open, a tree that sways in the wind answers every gust by laying down what botanists call stress wood, or reaction wood, denser fibers placed exactly where the strain falls, and by pushing its roots deeper into the ground. The wind that pushes against a tree is also what teaches it to stand. The Biosphere trees had been spared every storm, and so they never learned how to remain.

Filipinos understand this better than most. Anyone who has watched an old mango tree in the province ride out a strong typhoon, losing leaves and smaller branches but still standing the next morning, has seen something deep at work beneath the soil. The twelfth chapter of Hebrews closes with a picture of God shaking the whole world, and it turns out to be one of the most comforting passages in the New Testament.

The letter was written to Jewish believers in Jesus who were tired and under pressure. They had endured public insult and the seizure of their property (Hebrews 10:32–34), and some were tempted to slip quietly back into the familiar world of the temple and its sacrifices. Just before our passage, the writer reminds them that God disciplines the children he loves (Hebrews 12:5–11) and warns them against becoming like Esau, who traded his inheritance for a single meal (Hebrews 12:16). Then, to show them what they would be walking away from, the writer takes them to two mountains.

The first is Sinai, painted the way Israel remembered it. For three days the people had washed their clothes and waited behind a boundary that no one, not even an animal, was allowed to cross (Exodus 19:10–13). On the third morning, thunder and lightning broke over the mountain, a thick cloud settled on its peak, and a trumpet blast grew louder and louder until everyone in the camp trembled (Exodus 19:16–19). Smoke billowed up like the smoke from a furnace. When God spoke, the people could not bear it, and they “begged that no further word be spoken to them” (Hebrews 12:19). Even Moses, the man who spoke with God as a friend, confessed, “I am trembling with fear” (Hebrews 12:21).

Then the scene changes. “But you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,” the writer says. “You have come to thousands upon thousands of angels in joyful assembly, to the church of the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven” (Hebrews 12:22–23). The Greek word behind “joyful assembly” is panēgyris, the word Greeks used for a public festival, the kind of crowded, music-filled celebration that drew whole cities into the streets. The same holy God who blazed on Sinai is present on Zion, and the difference lies in how his people now come near: through “Jesus the mediator of a new covenant,” whose sprinkled blood “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). Abel’s blood cried out from the ground for justice (Genesis 4:10). The blood of Jesus speaks mercy, and it welcomes trembling people into the celebration.

Having brought them to the festival, the writer adds a sober warning: “See to it that you do not refuse him who speaks” (Hebrews 12:25). Then comes a promise borrowed from the prophet Haggai.

“At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, ‘Once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.’ The words ‘once more’ indicate the removing of what can be shaken (that is, created things), so that what cannot be shaken may remain. Therefore, since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us be thankful, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe, for our ‘God is a consuming fire.’” (Hebrews 12:26–29)

The original setting of that quotation changes how the whole passage feels. Around 520 BC, a small band of exiles back from Babylon was rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem, and the older people among them were heartbroken by how plain it looked. God asked them through Haggai, “Does it not seem to you like nothing?” (Haggai 2:3). His answer to those discouraged builders was this very promise of shaking, followed by the words, “The glory of this present house will be greater than the glory of the former house” (Haggai 2:9). In its first setting, the shaking was good news for people who felt small.

Hebrews draws out what the shaking is for. The phrase “the removing of what can be shaken” uses the Greek word metathesis, a word for transferring something or taking it away, and its purpose is stated plainly: “so that what cannot be shaken may remain.” The word for “cannot be shaken” is asaleutos. Luke uses it in Acts 27:41 for the moment Paul’s ship ran aground, when “the bow stuck fast and would not move” even as the surf pounded the stern to pieces. After the storm has done everything it can, something is still lodged firmly in place. If, as many scholars think, Hebrews was written before the Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70, its first readers were only a few years away from watching the stones they had trusted come down, while the kingdom they had received in Jesus would still be standing.

One way to read this passage is that God’s shaking works as a kind of sorting. Whatever is merely created, however impressive, can be loosened and carried off, while whatever belongs to his kingdom holds. The wind does similar work on a tree, stripping away dead branches while it drives the roots deeper and thickens the wood where the strain is greatest. When God shakes your life, he is sorting it, clearing away what was never strong enough to hold you so that what cannot be shaken may remain.

Most of us can name something that has been shaken this year. It may be a job that suddenly ended, a frightening diagnosis, a friendship that cooled, or savings that a single hospital bill emptied. Those losses are real, and Scripture never asks us to pretend otherwise. Hebrews invites us, though, to look at what is still standing after the wind passes, especially the welcome of Jesus, whose blood speaks mercy over you, and a name written in heaven that no crisis can erase.

The response the writer asks for may surprise us. Since we are “receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken,” the first instruction is simply “let us be thankful” (Hebrews 12:28). The verb “receiving” is in the present tense, which suggests the kingdom is being placed in our hands even now, in the middle of the trembling, and gratitude is how our roots go down to meet it. A good way to begin is to sit with a notebook tonight and write two lines side by side, one thing that was shaken loose from you this year and, beside it, one thing God kept firm. Thank him for the second line by name, and then offer him the first.

The chapter ends with a line from Deuteronomy 4:24: “our God is a consuming fire.” At Sinai that fire kept the people at a distance, and on Zion, for all who come through Jesus, the same fire becomes the warmth at the center of the festival, burning away what is temporary and keeping everything that is truly his. You need not fear the wind moving through your life this season. Let it drive your roots deeper, hold on to the One who is holding you, and when the morning comes you will find that you are still standing.

articles.title: The Day Someone Clapped for Bad News
articles.dek: Ezekiel's exiles blamed their parents for everything. God's answer sounded stern at first, and then it turned out to be the most hopeful sentence in the room.
articles.quote: God is the one at the head of the table who would rather hear your honest red today than lose you to a page of comfortable green.
articles.body:
In the autumn of 2006, an engineer named Alan Mulally left Boeing to run the Ford Motor Company, and he walked into a company that was bleeding badly. Ford would post a loss of $12.7 billion that year, the worst in its long history. Mulally set up a weekly meeting he called the Business Plan Review, and every Thursday his senior executives had to report on their work using charts marked in three colors: green for on track, yellow for trouble ahead, and red for a serious problem.

For weeks, every chart in the room came in green. The company was losing billions, yet each leader at the table reported that his own corner was fine. Journalist Bryce Hoffman, who told the story in his book American Icon, describes Mulally finally pointing out the obvious and asking whether anything at all was going badly. Nobody spoke. At the old Ford, admitting a problem was how careers ended, and every man at that table had learned the lesson from the executives who came before him.

Then Mark Fields, who ran the Americas division, took a risk. The launch of the new Ford Edge had been held up by a mechanical problem at a plant in Ontario, and he marked it red. Some of his colleagues assumed he would soon be gone. Instead, Mulally began to clap. By Hoffman's account he said, "Mark, that is great visibility," and then asked the room who could help. Someone offered a fix almost at once. The next week the charts arrived in honest shades of yellow and red, and for the first time Ford could see its real condition. Two years later, when the financial crisis hit, Ford came through without the emergency government rescue that its two Detroit rivals needed.

The rules of the meeting stayed exactly the same that day. What changed was the face of the man at the head of the table. People will tell the truth about themselves once they believe the one listening wants them to survive.

Ezekiel 18 is about that same discovery, made under far heavier circumstances. Ezekiel was a priest carried off to Babylon in 597 BC, along with King Jehoiachin and thousands of Jerusalem's leading families. He prophesied to fellow exiles living by the Kebar River, people who had lost their homes, their land, and their temple worship. They were grieving, and they had found a way to explain their grief. It came in the form of a popular saying.

"What do you people mean by quoting this proverb about the land of Israel," God asks through the prophet, "'The parents eat sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge'?" (Ezekiel 18:2). The Hebrew word for sour grapes, boser, refers to unripe fruit, hard and green and sharp enough to make your jaw ache. The phrase "set on edge" translates a verb that means to be blunted or dulled, the way your teeth feel after biting a green mango. The proverb meant that the older generation had done the sinning and the younger generation was paying for it. Jeremiah heard the same saying back in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 31:29). It was the national mood in a single line, and it had a measure of truth in it, since the sins of earlier kings like Manasseh really had brought ruin on the land.

The trouble was what the proverb did to the people repeating it. It turned their whole situation into somebody else's chart. If the grapes were eaten long ago, then the present generation had nothing to examine, nothing to confess, and nothing to change. It sounded humble, yet it carried a quiet accusation underneath, one the people eventually said aloud: "The way of the Lord is not just" (Ezekiel 18:25).

God answers with an oath. "As surely as I live, declares the Sovereign LORD, you will no longer quote this proverb in Israel. For everyone belongs to me, the parent as well as the child" (Ezekiel 18:3–4). Then he walks the exiles through a case study spanning three generations. A righteous man lives by God's ways. His son turns violent and cruel, and that son must answer for his own choices. Then comes a grandson, and Ezekiel describes him with great care: he "sees all the sins his father commits, and though he sees them, he does not do such things" (Ezekiel 18:14). That grandson, God says, "will not die for his father's sin; he will surely live" (Ezekiel 18:17).

On a first reading the chapter can feel like a courtroom, with every person standing alone before the judge. Yet the longer you stay with it, the clearer it becomes that God is pleading. Halfway through he stops and asks a question that reveals his heart:

"Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? declares the Sovereign LORD. Rather, am I not pleased when they turn from their ways and live?" (Ezekiel 18:23)

This is the moment Mulally clapped. The exiles had been holding up green charts, insisting that every failure belonged to their fathers. God responds by telling them that their lives are their own, and in the same breath he reveals that he longs for them to mark something red so they can live. Personal responsibility in this chapter is the doorway to hope. If your teeth are permanently dulled by your grandfather's grapes, nothing you do today could matter. If your life belongs to God and to no one else, a turn is possible this very afternoon.

The word Ezekiel uses again and again for that turn is shuv, the ordinary Hebrew verb for turning around on a road and heading back the other way. And God promises that the turn is complete: "None of the offenses they have committed will be remembered against them" (Ezekiel 18:22). The chapter closes with God practically calling across the distance to his people: "Rid yourselves of all the offenses you have committed, and get a new heart and a new spirit. Why will you die, people of Israel? For I take no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Sovereign LORD. Repent and live!" (Ezekiel 18:31–32).

It can seem strange that God would command people to produce a new heart, as though they could manufacture one. Eighteen chapters later, Ezekiel delivers the answer to that puzzle, when God says, "I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you" (Ezekiel 36:26). One way to read the two passages together is that the command in chapter 18 is an invitation to want what God has already promised to give. Our part is the turning, and his part is the remaking.

Many Filipino families know the sour-grapes proverb in their own words. We say a son is manang-mana sa tatay, just like his father, and sometimes we mean the temper, the drinking, or the habit of walking away. We say "ganyan talaga kami," that's just how our family is, and the phrase quietly closes the door on change. Ezekiel 18 honors the grandson who sees clearly what was handed to him and chooses a different road. He does not have to pretend his father was perfect, and he does not have to carry his father's verdict either. He belongs to God, and so do you.

Every one of us has some area of life we keep reporting as green. God is the one at the head of the table who would rather hear your honest red today than lose you to a page of comfortable green. Sometime before you sleep tonight, name one thing to him plainly, without blaming the people who taught it to you, and then expect the response Ezekiel describes, which is a Father leaning toward you with help already in hand. And when someone in your home or your workplace finally finds the courage to tell you their own bad news, you will know how to answer, because you will have just been answered that way yourself.

articles.title: The One Who Signs Beside Your Name
articles.dek: Hidden in Psalm 119 is a quiet banking word, the language of a co-maker on a loan. A weary servant used it to ask God to stand in for him, and the prayer is still open to anyone who is tired.
articles.quote: When God signs his name beside yours, your weakness becomes his responsibility, and you never again have to run the last stretch alone.
articles.body:
On a summer evening in 1992, in the Olympic stadium in Barcelona, a British sprinter named Derek Redmond settled into the blocks for the 400-meter semifinal. He had fought his way back from a long run of injuries and operations, and many people believed this was finally his race. About halfway down the back straight, something in the back of his right leg snapped. His hamstring had torn, and he went down onto one knee on the track while the other runners pulled away toward the finish.

Medics hurried over with a stretcher, but Redmond waved them off. He stood up and began to hop, crying from pain and heartbreak, determined to finish. High in the stands his father, Jim, was already moving. He pushed through the crowd, slipped past the officials who tried to stop him, and reached his son on the track. He put an arm around Derek's waist, and Derek leaned his whole weight onto his father's shoulder. By most accounts, Jim told him that he did not have to do this, and when Derek said he had to finish, his father answered that they would finish it together. They limped down the home straight side by side while some 65,000 people rose to their feet. Near the line, Jim stepped back so his son could cross it himself. The official record lists Derek Redmond as "did not finish," yet the race is remembered around the world as one of the most moving moments in Olympic history.

Hold that picture of a father coming down from the stands, because a very old prayer asks God to do almost exactly that.

Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible. It has 176 verses arranged in twenty-two stanzas of eight lines, one stanza for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and every line in a stanza begins with that stanza's letter. Today's section belongs to the letter ayin, a word that also means "eye." It fits, because this is a stanza about a man who has been watching and waiting for a long time. "My eyes fail, looking for your salvation, looking for your righteous promise" (Psalm 119:123). He is surrounded by people the psalm calls "the arrogant," people who ignore God and press hard on anyone who doesn't. He has tried to live rightly: "I have done what is righteous and just; do not leave me to my oppressors" (Psalm 119:121). Still, the pressure has not lifted, and his strength is running low. Then, in the second line of the stanza, he prays something unusual.

"Ensure your servant's well-being; do not let the arrogant oppress me." (Psalm 119:122)

The NIV's "ensure your servant's well-being" is a faithful translation, but the Hebrew verb underneath it carries a texture worth knowing. The word is 'arab, and it belongs to the world of loans and pledges. It means to stand surety for someone, to put your own name and property behind another person's debt. Older English Bibles render it "be surety for thy servant." Filipinos know the idea well. It is what a co-maker does at the bank or the lending cooperative when he signs his name below a cousin's on a motorcycle loan, promising that if the borrower cannot pay, the lender may come to him.

The same word appears at one of the tenderest moments in Genesis. Joseph, still unrecognized by his brothers, has demanded that they bring young Benjamin down to Egypt, and old Jacob cannot bear to let the boy go. Judah steps forward and says, "I myself will guarantee his safety; you can hold me personally responsible for him" (Genesis 43:9). Later, when Benjamin seems lost, Judah offers to become a slave in his place (Genesis 44:33). That is what 'arab looks like with skin on: one person placing himself between another and the thing that would crush him.

The Bible is honest that standing surety is costly, and it usually advises caution. "Whoever puts up security for a stranger will surely suffer, but whoever refuses to shake hands in pledge is safe" (Proverbs 11:15). Wise people hesitate to sign for someone else's debts. Against that background, the psalmist's prayer becomes quietly bold. He asks the Lord to do the very thing careful people avoid: to sign beside his name, to take on his liability, and to stand between him and those who would take everything from him.

There is one more detail that makes this line glow. Almost every verse of Psalm 119 mentions God's word under one of its many names: law, statutes, precepts, decrees, commands, promise. Verse 122 is one of the very few that does not. One way to read this is that, at his most pressed moment, the psalmist reaches past the page to the Person behind it. He loves Scripture deeply (he will say in verse 127 that he loves God's commands "more than gold, more than pure gold"), but in this breath he asks for God himself to come and stand with him.

Three times in these eight lines he calls himself "your servant" (Psalm 119:122, 124, 125). He is not claiming to be strong. He is reminding God whose he is, and he leans on God's character to carry the rest: "Deal with your servant according to your love" (Psalm 119:124). The word for love there is hesed, God's loyal, covenant-keeping kindness, the love that stays and pays.

Centuries later, the writer of Hebrews reached for the same idea to describe what Jesus has done. "Because of this oath, Jesus has become the guarantor of a better covenant" (Hebrews 7:22). The prayer of Psalm 119:122 found its fullest answer in a Son who came down from heaven onto the track of our broken lives, put his shoulder under our weight, and took our debt as his own. When God signs his name beside yours, your weakness becomes his responsibility, and you never again have to run the last stretch alone.

Perhaps you know what it is to be the psalmist this week. You have tried to do what is right at work, at home, or in a difficult relationship, and the pressure has not eased. Maybe there is a literal debt that keeps you awake, or a family burden you have carried for years as the dependable one, the one everyone else leans on. It is easy to believe that faith means gritting your teeth and hopping toward the finish on one good leg. This psalm gives you permission to pray differently, and to ask the Lord, in plain words, to stand surety for you in the specific place where you are most exposed.

You might take a few minutes today, perhaps on the jeepney ride or before you sleep, and name that one burden out loud to God. Then pray verse 122 in your own words: "Lord, I am your servant. Please sign beside my name here. Stand between me and what I cannot carry." After that, rest in the truth that you have handed the liability to Someone who is fully able to pay it. Jim Redmond could carry his son only as far as the finish line, and he could not heal the torn muscle. Your Guarantor has already paid the debt in full, and he walks with you well past the line.

The psalmist ends this stanza with his eyes still open and his heart still steady: "I consider all your precepts right" (Psalm 119:128). He has not seen every answer yet, but he has placed his name beside God's, and that is enough to keep going. May the same be true for you today, as you lean your full weight on the One who came down from the stands to finish the race with you.

articles.title: What Your Eyes Already Know
articles.dek: A scientist's wife saw something in his eyes that he couldn't hide. Proverbs says our heavenly Father watches for the same thing, and asks for it gently.
articles.quote: Whatever holds your heart will soon hold your eyes, so give your heart to the Father who has already given you his Son.
articles.body:
One evening around 1960, Eckhard Hess was lying in bed paging through a book of animal photographs. Hess was a respected psychologist at the University of Chicago who studied how animals and people perceive the world, so a book of striking wildlife pictures was ordinary bedtime reading for him. As he later told the story, his wife glanced over and said something that puzzled him: his pupils were unusually large. Hess pointed out that the lamp was bright and the light in the room had not changed. She was quite sure of what she had seen.

Hess carried that small remark into his laboratory, and it shaped years of his career. Working with his colleague James Polt, he showed volunteers a series of pictures while carefully measuring the width of their pupils, keeping the brightness of each image the same. The results, published in the journal Science in 1960, were striking. The pupil widened when a person looked at something that genuinely interested or delighted them. Among the women in the study, some of the strongest responses came from a picture of a baby and a picture of a mother holding her child. The eye, it turned out, was quietly reporting on the heart, and it did so whether its owner intended it or not.

Researchers have refined Hess's methods since then, and pupil measurement is now a standard tool in studies of attention, effort, and emotion. The heart of his discovery has held up well: what we love draws our eyes, and our eyes open wider to take it in. Long before any laboratory existed, a father in ancient Israel seems to have understood the same thing.

Proverbs 23 sits inside a section the book itself calls "the sayings of the wise" (Proverbs 22:17), a collection of short teachings shaped like a parent's counsel to a grown child who is about to step out into the world. The tone of our passage is warm, almost pleading. "Listen to your father, who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old" (Proverbs 23:22). Then comes a line about value: "Buy the truth and do not sell it, wisdom, instruction and insight as well" (23:23). Truth is worth paying for, and once you own it, nothing on the market should tempt you to trade it away.

Next the father speaks openly about his own joy. "The father of a righteous child has great joy; a man who fathers a wise son rejoices in him. May your father and mother rejoice; may she who gave you birth be joyful!" (23:24–25). Any Filipino parent who has sat in a crowded gymnasium on graduation day, waving at a child in a toga, knows the feeling these verses describe. A child's wisdom becomes a gift returned to the people who raised them. Having said all this, the father makes one request.

"My son, give me your heart and let your eyes delight in my ways." (Proverbs 23:26)

In Hebrew thought the heart, lev, is the command center of the whole person. It is where a person thinks and chooses as well as where they feel, so the father is asking for the place where every other decision begins. Proverbs says the same thing elsewhere: "Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it" (Proverbs 4:23). The father wants the source, because he knows the streams will follow.

The order of his request is the quiet surprise of this verse. He asks for the heart first, and he expects the eyes to come along on their own, much as the pupils of Hess's volunteers widened without any effort at the things they loved. There is a small and lovely detail in the Hebrew manuscripts here. The written text uses a verb meaning "delight in," while the ancient scribes noted in the margin a similar-looking verb meaning "keep" or "watch closely." The NIV follows the first reading, and some other translations follow the second. Both readings point in the same direction, toward eyes that study the father's ways closely because the heart behind them loves him.

Why the father presses this so tenderly becomes clear in the next lines. "For an adulterous woman is a deep pit, and a wayward wife is a narrow well. Like a bandit she lies in wait and multiplies the unfaithful among men" (23:27–28). Ancient Israelites cut cisterns into the limestone to catch rainwater, and many were shaped like a bottle, with a narrow mouth opening into a wide chamber below. Such a pit was easy to fall into and almost impossible to climb out of without help from above. The prophet Jeremiah was once lowered into one, "and Jeremiah sank down into the mud" (Jeremiah 38:6), until friends "pulled him up with the ropes and lifted him out of the cistern" (38:13).

The father's defense against that narrow well is a love strong enough to hold the eyes. He understands that the surest guard against a deadly delight is a deeper delight. His warning is about sexual unfaithfulness, and that danger is real in every generation, yet the same pattern shows up in many other pits. A phone glowing at midnight, an online gambling app that promises one more lucky round, and a grudge we keep replaying in our minds all work the same way. Each begins when the eyes linger, and each tightens its grip as the heart follows.

Here the gospel shines through this ancient proverb. The Father who asks for our heart is the same God who gave his own Son for us, and many of us are reading this from somewhere near the bottom of a narrow well. Proverbs can warn us about the pit, but only God can reach down into it. David wrote of that rescue with deep gratitude: "He lifted me out of the slimy pit, out of the mud and mire; he set my feet on a rock and gave me a firm place to stand" (Psalm 40:2). In Jesus, God came down into our mud, carried our unfaithfulness to the cross, and rose to lift us out. He even meets the request of Proverbs 23:26 from his own side, promising through Ezekiel, "I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you" (Ezekiel 36:26).

Jesus taught the same connection that Hess stumbled upon in his bedroom. "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also," he said, and in the very next breath, "The eye is the lamp of the body" (Matthew 6:21–22). Your eyes are honest witnesses, which makes them a gentle and useful mirror. One practical way to live this passage is to pay attention this week to where your eyes drift when nobody is asking anything of them, on the jeepney, in the queue, in the last minutes before sleep. That drift will tell you what your heart is reaching for, and it will show you where to bring your heart back to God.

From there, the way forward is to turn your eyes toward a better delight. Hebrews describes the Christian life as "fixing our eyes on Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of faith" (Hebrews 12:2). Tonight, before you reach for the phone, you might open to a single psalm, read it slowly, and pray in plain words, "Father, here is my heart. Teach my eyes to delight in your ways." Whatever holds your heart will soon hold your eyes, so give your heart to the Father who has already given you his Son.

Remember, too, the joy in verses 24 and 25. The father in Proverbs is no stern inspector waiting to catch his child failing. He is a parent in the bleachers, hoping and cheering, ready to rejoice. Your heavenly Father looks at you in Christ with that same gladness, and when you hand him your heart, even a tired and wandering one, his delight in you does the rest of the work.
